# R03 interrupted local-process recovery discussion

## Current question and authority

On 2026-11-07 the user parked documentation organization and left CRED-03-04 in place to discuss R03. The user selected the direction of preserving unknown effects without automatic replay. UI presentation and whether managed OCR and arbitrary scripts should share recovery remain undecided. This is discussion only: no spec, tickets, selected R03 batch, implementation or execution is authorized.

The [runtime recovery boundaries](../design/RUNTIME_AND_DELIVERY.md#recovery-boundaries) already require preserving useful work and stopping on unresolved local effects. [R03 evidence](../reviews/RUNTIME_FINDINGS.md#r03--local-process-stop-can-leave-no-supported-continuation) is inherited source-supported analysis, not a new Stop/reopen experiment. [Stage C](../PHASE_PLAN.md#c-continue-through-ordinary-interruptions) distinguishes managed OCR from opt-in host scripts. No code or runtime state was inspected in this discussion; feasibility remains unverified. External research is outside this discussion's access scope, so the recommendations below are conceptual proposals rather than a selected implementation design.

## UI comparison

Assistant proposals, not user-adopted choices:

| Option | Benefit | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A concise blocked-state notice with expandable evidence | A reader first sees which operation is unresolved, why Continue is blocked and where preserved work is accessible; detailed identities, last durable boundary and logs remain inspectable. | Needs careful wording so process termination is not mistaken for rollback or proof of no effects. |
| A detailed recovery panel shown immediately | Makes operation identity, known outputs, unresolved effects and available evidence visible together. | More cognitive load; technical detail can obscure the immediate task and can imply that every listed action is safe. |

Assistant recommendation: compare a concise notice plus expandable evidence first. For an interrupted OCR example, proposed wording is: “OCR was interrupted. Its effects are not fully known. Saved work is preserved; this operation will not be repeated automatically.” This is illustrative copy, not agreed UI text or a spec. A killed process alone does not prove descendants stopped, output completeness or absence of external effects. Do not display “not run”, “rolled back”, “safe to retry” or a success verdict without corresponding evidence. A generic Continue/Retry button must not silently authorize replay. Whether to expose evidence inspection, explicit successor work, acknowledgement or other actions is still open; no action is assumed available today.

## Managed OCR and arbitrary scripts

Assistant proposals, not user-adopted choices:

| Option | Benefit | Tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One conservative recovery flow for both | A consistent blocked-state explanation and a common prohibition on blind replay. | Either leaves recoverable managed work blocked or treats script effects as more knowable than the app can establish. |
| Shared uncertainty/preservation rules, operation-specific reconciliation | Common truthfulness and evidence access; managed OCR may later exploit app-owned inputs, output identities and validated receipts, while scripts retain unknown host/external effects. | Requires explicit proof boundaries per operation, more checks and a UI that explains why available actions differ. |

Assistant recommendation: share the meaning of unknown effects, work preservation and the no-automatic-replay rule; compare different recovery mechanisms underneath. Managed OCR is a candidate for reconciling already completed results or an explicitly selected isolated successor, only after checking output ownership, cache writes, publication and process/descendant boundaries. Being in its own directory is insufficient. Arbitrary scripts run with host-user permissions after opt-in; arbitrary file writes, descendants and external actions cannot be inferred absent from termination or missing output. Process-level script opt-in is not proof of replay safety. A common visible status need not imply identical recovery actions.

Reconciliation of a durable completed result differs from repeating an operation. A new operation identity must not erase the original unknown operation, its useful files or consumption. Whether any successor is offered, its authority and how it coexists with an unresolved original remain open. No automatic successor is proposed as a workaround for the user's no-replay direction.

## Resume questions

1. Should the first UI view emphasize a short task-oriented explanation with expandable evidence, or show the recovery evidence panel immediately? Which facts and available actions must be visible without expansion?
2. Should recovery share only the uncertainty/preservation rules while separating OCR and script mechanisms, or use one conservative blocked flow? What evidence would justify making any managed OCR action available?

Next activity is continued comparison of these two questions. Neither choice has been agreed, and no spec or implementation follows without a later instruction selecting that activity. These conceptual examples do not establish product capability or planned acceptance. Keep the existing work disposition and phase acceptance unchanged.

## Documentation checks

This discussion adds a topic owner, its catalogue route and a precise continuation pointer. Existing runtime rules, phase conditions, finding evidence, work selection and batch files remain unchanged. `python -B tools/docs/check_docs.py` passed with no errors: 117 Markdown files, 5,564 local links/destinations, 356 preserved points/detail mappings, 275 source dispositions and 503 bundled-source files. A semantic reread confirmed that user direction, assistant recommendations and unresolved choices remain distinct, with parked-work return links and no selected R03 batch. These checks do not establish runtime behavior; no application checks, provider/private-data access, installation, Git operation or external action is part of this discussion.
